relationships.label: Founding member claimed by Oglesby
relationships.description: Oglesby explicitly calls Ford a founding Bilderberg member while discussing his acceptability to competing elite factions. This is retained as the source’s claimed membership and is not independent verification of a founding roster.

relationships.label: Member and associated researcher
relationships.description: In the body Oglesby explicitly includes himself among Assassination Information Bureau members presenting the Zapruder film. The author biography separately states that he was associated with the bureau.

relationships.label: Early president
relationships.description: The author biography identifies Oglesby as an early president of Students for a Democratic Society. This is an explicit organizational role, not inferred from his general antiwar writing.

relationships.label: Retired official
relationships.description: Oglesby explicitly introduces Copeland as a retired CIA official. His publications advocating surveillance and his allegations about Watergate are distinguished from that occupational affiliation.

relationships.label: CIA affiliation in Prouty’s interpretation
relationships.description: Oglesby reports Prouty’s description of Lansdale among CIA-linked hard-nosed liberals influencing policy in Vietnam. The affiliation and characterization remain attributed to that cited account.

relationships.label: Chief military adviser
relationships.description: Oglesby identifies Taylor as Kennedy’s chief military adviser in the discussion of Prouty’s criticism of Vietnam policy. This adds the adviser relationship beyond Taylor’s existing Joint Chiefs affiliation.

relationships.label: Commission chairman during1949–1950 controversy
relationships.description: Oglesby explicitly identifies Lilienthal as AEC chairman and recounts a senator’s accusation about atomic secrets, Lilienthal’s warning against military dominance and his resignation. The accusation is not encoded as a proven disclosure.

relationships.label: Orders thermonuclear development against commission advice
relationships.description: Oglesby describes Truman issuing the hydrogen-bomb go-ahead against AEC advice. The passage’s February 1,1950 date differs from Quigley’s January 31 account; the policy relationship is represented without silently reconciling the date.

relationships.label: Wartime intelligence command relationship
relationships.description: Oglesby describes Gehlen as part of Hitler’s general staff and head of Soviet intelligence work. The source also recounts Gehlen proposing a role for Vlassov to Hitler, who rejected that proposal. This is a stated wartime relationship, not a postwar affiliation inferred from proximity.

relationships.label: Administration appointment and political alliance
relationships.description: Oglesby describes Nixon bringing Kissinger into government as an example of a president broadening support across his factional model. The appointment relationship is distinct from the author’s Yankee/Cowboy classifications.

relationships.label: National security leadership context
relationships.description: Oglesby refers to Kissinger’s National Security Council while comparing Haig’s joining it with Butterfield’s temporary military resignation. This is the source’s institutional identification, not evidence of a covert crash-related order.

relationships.label: Executive director/comptroller and later leadership
relationships.description: The Baker-report discussion quoted by Oglesby identifies Colby as executive director/comptroller supervising a secret Watergate-related inquiry, and the subsequent text notes his rise to agency leadership. This specifies office and investigation responsibility rather than assuming he directed the burglary.

relationships.label: Management leader and subsequent resignation
relationships.description: Oglesby names former Air Transport Command chief General Harold George as a Hughes Aircraft manager alongside Ramo and Wooldridge and recounts his resignation in the dispute with Hughes. The existing Quigley profile gives a different middle initial; career and institutional context support the same identity, but that discrepancy is flagged.

relationships.label: Contracting authority intervenes in management crisis
relationships.description: Oglesby describes Hughes Aircraft management threatening to complain to the Air Force over credit restrictions and Secretary Talbott intervening to protect Air Force contracts. This procurement and intervention connection is distinct from generic Pentagon dependence.

relationships.label: Commands agents during the Nevada takeover
relationships.description: Oglesby explicitly describes Davis commanding Intertel agents to take control of cashiers’ cages during the Hughes Nevada takeover. The source’s wider abduction and coup interpretations remain distinct from the reported security deployment.

relationships.label: Security deployment for the board-side takeover
relationships.description: Oglesby places Intertel agents under Davis’s command as Toolco took over Hughes’s Nevada operations. This adds the particular corporate-client deployment beyond the general ownership relationship with Resorts International.

relationships.label: Case-officer reporting and shared attorney fees
relationships.description: Oglesby quotes the Baker report describing Bennett’s report to his CIA case officer and the agency’s acknowledgment of paying half of his grand-jury attorney fee. This documents the cited contact and payment claim without treating every allegation of prior Watergate knowledge as proved.

relationships.label: Sensitive report transmitted through CIA case officer
relationships.description: Oglesby’s quoted Baker-report passage says the case officer’s account of Bennett’s Watergate information was carried to Helms on or before July 14,1972. The edge is a reported information channel, not proof Bennett and Helms jointly designed the burglary.

relationships.label: Personal and family security entrusted to McCord
relationships.description: Oglesby cites the Sunday Times team reporting that Mitchell entrusted his and his family’s security to McCord. This is an explicit client/protection relation; the author’s additional double-agent hypothesis remains contested.

relationships.label: Security Research Staff investigation role
relationships.description: Oglesby’s Baker-report discussion identifies Gaynor with the CIA Security Research Staff’s internal Watergate work and mentions his later retirement. This specific investigative role supplements the existing basic agency affiliation.

relationships.label: Inner-adviser circle reported
relationships.description: Oglesby lists Clifford among the Trilateral figures in Carter’s innermost adviser circle. The advisory association is source-reported and does not establish corporate ownership of the presidency.

relationships.label: Inner-adviser circle reported
relationships.description: Oglesby lists Ball among the additional Trilateral figures in Carter’s inner adviser circle. The book’s larger establishment-control explanation remains interpretive.

relationships.label: 1957 loan and regulatory-benefit interpretation
relationships.description: Oglesby describes the 205,000-dollar loan benefiting Nixon’s brother Donald and enumerates favorable regulatory decisions for Hughes interests. The author presents a reciprocal-benefit explanation; the edge preserves that interpretation rather than asserting a proved bribe.

relationships.label: Acquisition and large shareholding
relationships.description: Oglesby describes Hughes acquiring predecessor airlines in 1939, combining them into TWA and controlling 70 percent of its stock. This adds the explicit ownership and formation role to the earlier generic association; it does not settle the later dispute over management control.

relationships.label: Conditional ownership comparison
relationships.description: Oglesby writes that Chemical Bank and Morgan Guarantee Trust may own General Dynamics while most major plants lie in the Sunbelt. Conditional wording is preserved; no precise ownership percentage or independently verified holding is supplied.

relationships.label: Conditional ownership comparison
relationships.description: Oglesby writes that First National Bank of Boston and Girard Trust may own Lockheed while its plants lie in California, Texas and Georgia. This is the source’s conditional financial-geography comparison, not a verified controlling-shareholder finding.

relationships.label: Conditional ownership comparison
relationships.description: Oglesby names Girard Trust in the conditional Lockheed ownership comparison. The institution is distinct from New York’s Guaranty Trust, and the source supplies no shareholding percentage.

relationships.label: 1960 presidential running mate
relationships.description: Oglesby explicitly describes the Massachusetts Lodge as Nixon’s running mate in 1960. This is the younger diplomat, not the earlier senator who advocated Cuban intervention before 1898.

relationships.label: American participant identified in the source
relationships.description: Oglesby’s Quigley-based account lists Walter Lippmann in the American Round Table group and later calls him a secret Round Table member while recounting his criticism of Republican foreign policy. This is a source-reported roster claim, not an independently authenticated membership register.

relationships.label: Financial contributions attributed through Quigley
relationships.description: Oglesby, quoting Quigley’s account, names Carnegie United Kingdom Trust among substantial contributors to the Round Table network from 1925 onward. The institutional funding claim is distinguished from personal membership and remains attributed to the cited source.

relationships.label: Former bureau service
relationships.description: Oglesby explicitly describes Liddy as formerly of the FBI while contrasting the Watergate participants’ backgrounds. Former employment is distinct from the contested claim that the agency directed either the burglary or the arrests.

relationships.label: Alliance intelligence organization in Oglesby’s account
relationships.description: Oglesby claims the Gehlen organization became NATO’s official intelligence organization soon after the alliance formed. The institutional claim remains attributed and is not an independently verified monopoly over every NATO intelligence function.

relationships.label: Proposed loan from aircraft-company funds
relationships.description: Oglesby describes a government reversal allowing a 5-million-dollar Hughes loan to TWA from Hughes Aircraft funds. This records the approved financing proposal in the source’s regulatory-benefit account, without asserting that the loan was fully executed or proving the author’s broader quid-pro-quo theory.

relationships.label: Crash-investigation tape assessment and agency notification
relationships.description: In the Ruckelshaus letter quoted by Oglesby, FAA tower personnel invited an FBI agent to listen to crash-related tapes and agreed with his identification of the stall-warning sound, notifying FAA headquarters. The institutional exchange is distinct from the author’s later tape-tampering speculation.

relationships.label: Vietnam bombing plans and presidential orders
relationships.description: Oglesby describes Johnson signing marching orders reflecting detailed JCS plans for bombing the North before the public escalation in 1965. This is the author’s account of planning and authorization, distinct from his separate theory about elite motives.

relationships.label: Democratic presidential coalition in1960
relationships.description: Oglesby explicitly places Kennedy’s 1960 coalition with Johnson within the Democratic Party. The electoral party relationship is distinct from the author’s Yankee/Cowboy model and theories about later violence.

relationships.label: Democratic coalition partner
relationships.description: Oglesby describes Johnson as Kennedy’s 1960 coalition partner associated with the party’s right-wing elements. This records the stated party and electoral context without presenting an informal faction as a formal organization.

profileUpdates.description: Oglesby introduces Miles Copeland as a retired CIA official and analyzes his 1973 National Review argument for community surveillance. The later Watergate chapter contrasts Copeland’s claim that McCord trapped the burglars with agency testimony denying prior knowledge or a trap; neither claim is treated as established solely because Copeland once served in the CIA.

Oglesby cites Prouty in identifying Edward Lansdale as a CIA-connected figure whose Vietnam policy role is contrasted with Ellsberg’s account. The text also says Ellsberg worked for Lansdale in Vietnam; the larger Secret Team theory remains Prouty’s and Oglesby’s interpretation.

Oglesby identifies Lilienthal as Atomic Energy Commission chairman during the controversy after the Soviet atomic explosion. He recounts an accusation about sharing secrets with Britain, Lilienthal’s opposition to military domination of foreign policy and his resignation; the espionage-related allegation remains an accusation.

Oglesby places Truman’s announcement of the Soviet atomic explosion and decision to proceed with hydrogen-bomb development in the emerging struggle over nuclear strategy. The account says the thermonuclear order went against AEC advice and gives February 1,1950, a date differing from the January 31 passage in Quigley.

In Oglesby’s narrative Hitler is the wartime political superior of Gehlen’s Soviet-intelligence apparatus. The book recounts his rejection of Gehlen’s proposal to appoint Vlassov to a projected government and Gehlen’s later effort to bargain with the Americans as Nazi Germany collapsed.

Oglesby discusses Mussolini’s violent suppression of the Sicilian Mafia as background to the wartime American restoration of local criminal influence. This is an adversarial historical relationship; the passage does not make Mussolini a member of Lansky’s later American network.

Oglesby places Kissinger in Nixon’s administration and treats his inclusion as an example of cross-faction coalition building. Elsewhere the book refers to Kissinger’s National Security Council; speculative claims of covert responsibility are distinguished from those administrative associations.

Oglesby’s Baker-report discussion identifies Colby as CIA executive director/comptroller during an internal Watergate-related inquiry. The book later notes his rise to agency leadership, while its theory about Nixon using appointments to purge rivals remains an interpretation rather than the definition of Colby’s office.

Oglesby identifies General Harold George, formerly Air Transport Command chief, as a leader of Hughes Aircraft management. He recounts the struggle over research facilities, credit and owner control, followed by George’s resignation. The passage supplies no middle initial; the existing Quigley record’s initial should not be treated as independently confirmed by this source.

Oglesby discusses Eisenhower’s role in the transition from training Cuban guerrillas to planning an invasion. The cited Haynes Johnson account questions how much Eisenhower participated and records Eisenhower’s own insistence that his administration had planned guerrilla training rather than an invasion; that disagreement is preserved.

Oglesby recounts Herbert Hoover’sApril 1950 speech advocating removal of Communist states from the United Nations and contrasts it with Walter Lippmann’s criticism. This is the former president, not FBI director J. Edgar Hoover, and a policy proposal does not establish employment or membership in the UN.

Oglesby mentions Hayden while describing Robert Kennedy’s 1968 coalition extending toward New Politics activists, with the explicit qualification “if not Tom Hayden.” The passage does not establish Hayden joined the campaign or had a formal role in the coalition.

Oglesby quotes Quigley’s distinction between older eastern wealth and new Southwest and Far West wealth, then uses it to develop his own Yankee/Cowboy model. His discussion treats the Eastern Establishment as an informal social and financial network, not an incorporated body with a fixed membership roster.

The author’s biography identifies Oglesby as an early SDS president and an associate of the Assassination Information Bureau, and the body explicitly includes him among AIB members presenting the Zapruder film. His authorship and those stated institutional roles are distinct from the book’s contested theories of elite conflict.

Oglesby discusses Ford’s commission membership and later role as an acceptable presidential successor across competing factions. A late passage also claims Ford was a founding Bilderberg member; that claimed founding status remains attributed to this source rather than independently verified.

Oglesby’s summary of Quigley lists Lippmann among the American Round Table group and later describes him as a Yankee publicist and secret Round Table member. The book quotes his criticism of Republican anti-Communist rhetoric and opposition to European aid, preserving that political argument separately from the source-reported network affiliation.

Oglesby’s Quigley-based account names Carnegie United Kingdom Trust among later financial contributors to the Round Table network. This is a specific institutional funding claim, not a statement that every Carnegie organization or trustee shared the same formal membership.

Oglesby discusses NATO in the postwar intelligence account and claims the Gehlen organization became an official alliance intelligence organization. The claim remains attributed; it does not establish that NATO and the CIA were the same body or that one source monopolized every intelligence service.

Oglesby identifies Liddy as a White House operative involved in proposed political burglaries and explicitly notes his earlier FBI service. His operational and funding contacts are separated from the author’s contested explanations of why the Watergate team was arrested.

summary: Screened all764 canonical people and organization identities against source-wide name, alias and ambiguous-surname leads across the390-page PDF, including identities without any Yankee account. Reviewed candidate affiliation sentences independently of existing citations and reread selected source passages. Added explicit roles and transactions missed by the previous profile-citation audit; rejected namesakes, publisher/location matches, ordinary-word aliases and co-occurrence without a stated relation. This is a complete candidate-screening pass with targeted body-text verification, not a claim that every page was manually reread or every possible OCR spelling recovered. A follow-up38-identity delta screening added Lippmann’s Round Table association and Carnegie United Kingdom Trust funding while rejecting the Straight, Whitney, Lamont and Field namesake/ordinary-word leads. A final short-form pass examined18 acronym/base-name hypotheses, rejected CTIA→CIA and British-industries→FBI expansions, and added specific Liddy-FBI, Gehlen-NATO, HAC-TWA, FBI-FAA and Johnson-JCS relations.

coverage.limits: All390 pages received automated name/alias and ambiguous-surname screening. All764 identity inventories and their candidate-page lists were screened.The initial pass reviewed explicit-affiliation sentences on106 pages, followed by candidate-context review for the38-identity delta; selected passages were read in fuller context. Notes and index mentions were separated from evidentiary body passages. Common surname leads remain ambiguous until a first name, role or institution identifies the individual. OCR, line breaks, incomplete corporate aliases and synonymous institution names can leave undetected passages; this pass does not certify exhaustive extraction of every affiliation in the book. The NSA/NSAM naming error and the Harold George middle-initial discrepancy are flagged rather than silently normalized. Context-page review includes broader body passages around the candidate, not an assertion that every sentence on each listed page was reread. The final short-form pass source-resolved18 identities and406 generated page leads; grouped false acronyms were rejected without treating their pages as manually reread.

shortFormScreening.limits: Generated acronym hypotheses were source-resolved first. The wrong CTIA→CIA and British-industries→FBI expansions were rejected as whole classes, without pretending to reread every CIA or FBI page. Valid recurring acronym leads were checked against existing source context and explicit-role passages. Newly reread body passages are recorded separately from all mechanically screened page leads.
